title: Chapter 3: Your First Python AI App
content:
Chapter 3: Your First Python AI App

Opening Hook: Turn Your LLM Client into a Real App

In Chapter 1, you built a simple Python code explainer.

In Chapter 2, you cleaned up your foundation by creating a reusable LLM client.

Now it is time to turn that foundation into your first real Python AI app.

Not just a single script.

Not just a one-off prompt.

A small but structured command-line assistant.

This app will let a user choose different AI tasks, such as:

/ask
/explain
/summarize
/tasks

The assistant will route the request, build the right prompt, call the model, and return a useful response.

This is an important step.

Many AI tutorials show one prompt and one response.

Real apps need structure.

A real app needs:

User input
↓
Command handling
↓
Prompt template
↓
LLM call
↓
Formatted response
↓
Next user action

That is what you will build in this chapter.

By the end, you will have a reusable command-line AI assistant that can answer questions, explain Python concepts, summarize text, and create task plans.

This is still beginner-friendly.

But it is no longer just a demo.

It is the beginning of an actual AI application.

What You Will Learn

By the end of this chapter, you will understand:

  • How to structure a small Python AI app
  • How input/output flow works in an AI assistant
  • How to use prompt templates
  • How to route user commands
  • How to create different assistant modes
  • How to format structured AI responses
  • How to reuse the LLM client from Chapter 2
  • How to test prompt builders and command parsing without live API calls
  • How to build a command-line assistant that feels useful

Why This Chapter Matters

A single AI function is easy to write.

A usable AI app needs organization.

Without structure, your project can quickly turn into:

random prompts
mixed API code
duplicate logic
hardcoded settings
unclear commands
untested functions

That may work for a few minutes, but it becomes difficult to maintain.

This chapter teaches a cleaner pattern:

llm_client.py → model access
prompts.py → prompt templates
commands.py → command parsing
assistant.py → app logic
app.py → user interface
tests → confidence
README.md → usability

This structure will prepare you for bigger projects later, including RAG apps, tool-using agents, memory assistants, and deployed web apps.

3.1 What Makes Something an AI App?

An AI app is not just a prompt.

An AI app combines AI with software behavior.

A simple AI app usually includes:

  • A user interface
  • Input validation
  • Prompt construction
  • A model call
  • Response formatting
  • Error handling
  • Repeated interaction

Your command-line assistant will have all of those pieces.

The interface will be the terminal.

The prompts will be stored in a separate file.

The model call will use your reusable client.

The app will continue running until the user exits.

That is the basic shape of many AI apps.

3.2 The Input/Output Flow

Your app will follow this flow:

User types command
↓
App parses command
↓
App selects prompt template
↓
App sends prompt to LLM
↓
LLM returns response
↓
App prints response
↓
User enters next command

For example:

User:
/explain Python dictionaries

Command parser:
command = /explain
content = Python dictionaries

Prompt builder:
Explain this Python concept for a beginner...

LLM:
Returns explanation

App:
Prints explanation

This is simple, but powerful.

The same pattern will appear again and again throughout this book.

3.3 Why Prompt Templates Matter

A prompt template is a reusable prompt with a variable part.

For example:

Explain the following Python concept for a beginner:

{concept}

The template stays the same.

The concept changes.

Prompt templates help because they make your app:

  • More consistent
  • Easier to test
  • Easier to improve
  • Easier to reuse
  • Easier to debug

Instead of writing prompts directly inside the app loop, you will store them in prompts.py.

That is cleaner.

3.4 Structured Responses

A structured response is an answer with predictable sections.

Weak instruction:

Explain this.

Better instruction:

Return your answer with these sections:
1. Short answer
2. Explanation
3. Example
4. Common mistake
5. Next step

Structured responses help the user.

They also help your app because predictable formatting is easier to evaluate later.

In Chapter 11, you will use required sections as part of AI evaluation.

So this habit starts now.

3.5 Project: Command-Line AI Assistant

What This Project Does

This project builds a terminal-based AI assistant with multiple modes.

It supports:

/help
/ask
/explain
/summarize
/tasks
/exit

Examples:

/ask What is RAG?

/explain Python list comprehensions

/summarize Python is a popular language because...

/tasks Build a PDF chatbot portfolio project

Who This Helps

This project helps:

  • Python learners
  • Students
  • Developers
  • Freelancers
  • AI beginners
  • Anyone who wants a practical first AI app

What You Will Build

OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini

On macOS or Linux:

On Windows PowerShell:

Then edit .env and add your real API key.

Never publish your real .env file.

3.8 File: llm_client.py

This is the reusable LLM client pattern from Chapter 2.

Create llm_client.py:

"""
Reusable LLM client for Chapter 3.

This client keeps provider-specific API logic separate from app logic.
"""

import os
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Protocol
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from openai import OpenAI

load_dotenv()

def get_env_float(name: str, default: float) -> float:
"""Read a float from an environment variable safely."""

raw_value = os.getenv(name)

if raw_value is None:
return default

try:
 return float(raw_value)
 except ValueError:
 return default

@dataclass
class LLMConfig:
"""Configuration for the LLM client."""

model: str = field(
 default_factory=lambda: os.getenv("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-4.1-mini")
 )
 temperature: float = field(
 default_factory=lambda: get_env_float("OPENAI_TEMPERATURE", 0.2)
 )

class LLMProvider(Protocol):
"""Protocol for LLM-like clients."""

def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
"""Return model-generated text."""
...

class LLMClient:
"""Reusable client for sending prompts to an LLM."""

def __init__(self, config: LLMConfig | None = None):
 self.config = config or LLMConfig()
 api_key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")

if not api_key:
raise ValueError(
"OPENAI_API_KEY is missing. Add it to your .env file."
)

self.client = OpenAI(api_key=api_key)

def build_input(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
"""Combine system and user messages into model input."""

if not system.strip():
 raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.")
if not user.strip():
 raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.")

return f"""
System instruction:
{system.strip()}

User request:
{user.strip()}
"""

def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
"""Send a request to the model and return text output."""

model_input = self.build_input(system=system, user=user)

response = self.client.responses.create(
model=self.config.model,
input=model_input,
temperature=self.config.temperature,
)

return response.output_text

class MockLLMClient:
"""Mock client for tests."""

def __init__(self, response_text: str = "Mock response"):
 self.response_text = response_text
 self.calls: list[dict[str, str]] = []

def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
"""Return a fixed response and record the call."""

if not system.strip():
 raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.")
if not user.strip():
 raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.")

self.calls.append(
{
"system": system,
"user": user,
}
)

return self.response_text

Not executed automatically: requires live API credentials, network access, or external service.

3.9 File: prompts.py

Create prompts.py.

This file stores prompt templates for each assistant mode.

"""
Prompt templates for the Chapter 3 command-line AI assistant.
"""

GENERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a helpful AI assistant for beginner-to-intermediate Python learners.

Be clear, practical, and honest.
Avoid unnecessary jargon.
Do not invent facts.
If you are unsure, say what is uncertain.
"""

PYTHON_TUTOR_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a friendly Python tutor.

Explain Python concepts clearly for beginner-to-intermediate learners.
Use simple examples.
Mention common mistakes when helpful.
Do not claim that you executed code unless execution actually happened.
"""

SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a careful summarization assistant.

Summarize only the text provided by the user.
Do not add facts that are not present in the text.
Keep the summary clear and useful.
"""

TASK_PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a practical task planning assistant.

Turn goals into clear, realistic task lists.
Do not overpromise.
Include human review when the task involves important decisions.
"""

def build_general_prompt(question: str) -> str:
"""Build a prompt for general questions."""

return f"""
Answer the following question clearly and practically:

{question}

Return:
1. Short answer
2. Explanation
3. Example or practical note
4. Next step
"""

def build_python_explanation_prompt(concept: str) -> str:
"""Build a prompt for explaining Python concepts."""

return f"""
Explain this Python concept for a beginner-to-intermediate learner:

{concept}

Return:
1. Simple definition
2. Why it matters
3. Short Python example
4. Common beginner mistake
5. Practice idea
"""

def build_summary_prompt(text: str) -> str:
"""Build a prompt for summarizing text."""

return f"""
Summarize the following text:

{text}

Return:
1. One-sentence summary
2. Key points
3. Important details
4. Suggested title

Rules:
- Use only the provided text.
- Do not invent information.
"""

def build_task_plan_prompt(goal: str) -> str:
"""Build a prompt for creating a task plan."""

return f"""
Create a practical task plan for this goal:

{goal}

Return:
Goal:
A short restatement of the goal.

Tasks:
A numbered list of clear steps.

Risks:
Possible risks or unclear areas.

Next Action:
The first action the user should take.

Rules:
- Keep the plan realistic.
- Do not invent deadlines, prices, or guarantees.
"""

3.10 File: commands.py

Create commands.py.

This file parses user commands.

"""
Command parsing for the Chapter 3 command-line AI assistant.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass

SUPPORTED_COMMANDS = {
"/help",
"/ask",
"/explain",
"/summarize",
"/tasks",
"/exit",
}

@dataclass
class ParsedCommand:
"""A parsed user command."""

command: str
content: str

def parse_command(user_input: str) -> ParsedCommand:
"""
Parse user input into a command and content.

If the user enters text without a slash command, treat it as /ask.
"""

cleaned = user_input.strip()

if not cleaned:
return ParsedCommand(command="", content="")

if not cleaned.startswith("/"):
return ParsedCommand(command="/ask", content=cleaned)

parts = cleaned.split(maxsplit=1)
 command = parts[0].lower()
 content = parts[1].strip() if len(parts) > 1 else ""

return ParsedCommand(command=command, content=content)

def is_supported_command(command: str) -> bool:
"""Return True if command is supported."""

return command in SUPPORTED_COMMANDS

def help_text() -> str:
"""Return command help text."""

return """
Available commands:

/help
Show this help message.

/ask [question]
Ask a general AI question.
Example: /ask What is RAG?

/explain [Python concept]
Explain a Python concept.
Example: /explain list comprehensions

/summarize [text]
Summarize provided text.
Example: /summarize Python is popular because...

/tasks [goal]
Create a task plan.
Example: /tasks Build a PDF chatbot

/exit
Quit the assistant.

Tip:
You can also type a normal question without a command.
It will be treated as /ask.
""".strip()

Test result: Python syntax check passed.

3.11 File: assistant.py

Create assistant.py.

This file connects commands, prompts, and the LLM client.

"""
Assistant logic for the Chapter 3 command-line AI app.
"""

from commands import parse_command, is_supported_command, help_text
from llm_client import LLMClient, LLMProvider
from prompts import (
GENERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
PYTHON_TUTOR_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
TASK_PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
build_general_prompt,
build_python_explanation_prompt,
build_summary_prompt,
build_task_plan_prompt,
)

def require_content(command: str, content: str) -> str | None:
"""
Return an error message if a command requires content and content is missing.
"""

if content.strip():
 return None

examples = {
"/ask": "Example: /ask What is RAG?",
"/explain": "Example: /explain Python dictionaries",
"/summarize": "Example: /summarize Paste text here.",
"/tasks": "Example: /tasks Build a PDF chatbot",
}

example = examples.get(command, "Please provide content.")

return f"Missing content for {command}.\n{example}"

def handle_command(
 user_input: str,
 client: LLMProvider | None = None,
) -> str:
 """
 Handle one user command and return assistant response.
 """

parsed = parse_command(user_input)

if not parsed.command:
return "Please enter a command or question."

if parsed.command == "/exit":
return "EXIT"

if parsed.command == "/help":
return help_text()

if not is_supported_command(parsed.command):
return f"Unknown command: {parsed.command}\nType /help to see available commands."

missing_message = require_content(parsed.command, parsed.content)

if missing_message:
return missing_message

llm = client or LLMClient()

if parsed.command == "/ask":
return llm.complete(
system=GENERAL_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
user=build_general_prompt(parsed.content),
)

if parsed.command == "/explain":
return llm.complete(
system=PYTHON_TUTOR_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
user=build_python_explanation_prompt(parsed.content),
)

if parsed.command == "/summarize":
return llm.complete(
system=SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
user=build_summary_prompt(parsed.content),
)

if parsed.command == "/tasks":
return llm.complete(
system=TASK_PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
user=build_task_plan_prompt(parsed.content),
)

return "Command was recognized but not handled."

Test result: Python syntax check passed.

3.12 File: app.py

Create app.py.

This is the command-line interface.

"""
Chapter 3 Project: Command-Line AI Assistant
"""

from assistant import handle_command

def print_welcome() -> None:
"""Print welcome message."""

print("\nCommand-Line AI Assistant")
print("=" * 45)
print("Type /help to see commands.")
print("Type /exit to quit.")
print("=" * 45)

def main() -> None:
"""Run the command-line assistant."""

print_welcome()

while True:
try:
user_input = input("\nYou: ").strip()

response = handle_command(user_input)

if response == "EXIT":
print("\nAssistant: Goodbye.")
break

print("\nAssistant:")
print(response)

except KeyboardInterrupt:
print("\n\nAssistant: Goodbye.")
break

except Exception as error:
print("\nAssistant:")
print(f"Something went wrong: {error}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
main()

3.15 File: test_assistant.py

These tests use the mock client.

They do not call the live API.

from assistant import handle_command, require_content
from llm_client import MockLLMClient
def test_require_content_returns_none_when_content_exists():
 result = require_content("/ask", "What is Python?")

assert result is None

def test_require_content_returns_error_when_missing():
 result = require_content("/ask", "")
assert "Missing content" in result
 assert "/ask" in result
def test_handle_help_command():
 response = handle_command("/help")
assert "Available commands" in response
 assert "/ask" in response
def test_handle_exit_command():
 response = handle_command("/exit")

assert response == "EXIT"

def test_handle_unknown_command():
 response = handle_command("/unknown test")

assert "Unknown command" in response

def test_handle_empty_input():
 response = handle_command(" ")

assert "Please enter" in response

def test_handle_ask_uses_mock_client():
 mock = MockLLMClient(response_text="Mock answer")

response = handle_command(
"/ask What is RAG?",
client=mock,
)

assert response == "Mock answer"
 assert len(mock.calls) == 1
 assert "What is RAG?" in mock.calls[0]["user"]
def test_handle_explain_uses_mock_client():
 mock = MockLLMClient(response_text="Mock explanation")

response = handle_command(
"/explain Python dictionaries",
client=mock,
)

assert response == "Mock explanation"
 assert len(mock.calls) == 1
 assert "Python dictionaries" in mock.calls[0]["user"]
def test_handle_summarize_uses_mock_client():
 mock = MockLLMClient(response_text="Mock summary")

response = handle_command(
"/summarize Python is useful for AI.",
client=mock,
)

assert response == "Mock summary"
 assert len(mock.calls) == 1
def test_handle_tasks_uses_mock_client():
 mock = MockLLMClient(response_text="Mock task plan")

response = handle_command(
"/tasks Build a chatbot",
client=mock,
)

assert response == "Mock task plan"
 assert len(mock.calls) == 1

3.17 How the Code Works

This app has five main layers.

Layer 1: User Interface

The app.py file handles terminal interaction.

It prints a welcome message, reads user input, calls handle_command(), and prints the response.

response = handle_command(user_input)

Test result: Python syntax check passed.

This keeps the interface simple.

Layer 2: Command Parsing

The commands.py file parses input.

Example:

/explain Python dictionaries

becomes:

ParsedCommand(
command="/explain",
content="Python dictionaries"
)

If the user types a normal question without a slash command, it becomes /ask.

Example:

What is RAG?

becomes:

ParsedCommand(
command="/ask",
content="What is RAG?"
)

This makes the assistant easier to use.

Layer 3: Prompt Templates

The prompts.py file stores prompt builders.

For example:

build_python_explanation_prompt("Python dictionaries")

Not executed automatically: requires live API credentials, network access, or external service.

returns a structured prompt asking the model to explain the concept with sections.

Layer 4: Assistant Logic

The assistant.py file connects commands to prompts.

If the command is /summarize, it uses:

SUMMARY_SYSTEM_PROMPT
build_summary_prompt(...)

Not executed automatically: requires live API credentials, network access, or external service.

If the command is /tasks, it uses:

TASK_PLANNER_SYSTEM_PROMPT
build_task_plan_prompt(...)

This routing is the heart of the app.

Layer 5: LLM Client

The llm_client.py file handles model access.

The assistant does not need to know provider details.

It simply calls:

llm.complete(system=..., user=...)

That separation makes the app cleaner.

3.18 Sample User Session

A typical session may look like this:

Command-Line AI Assistant
=============================================
Type /help to see commands.
Type /exit to quit.
=============================================

You: /explain Python dictionaries

Assistant:

Dictionaries are useful when you want to look up information by name or label.

print(person["name"])

4. Common beginner mistake

5. Practice idea

This is sample output only.

Do not claim exact output unless you run the code and capture the real result.

3.21 Why This Is Your First Real AI App

This app is simple, but it has real application structure.

It includes:

commands
prompt templates
assistant logic
model access
tests
documentation

That is much stronger than a one-file demo.

It also introduces a pattern you will reuse later:

Mode
↓
Prompt template
↓
Model call
↓
Structured output

In Chapter 4, the mode will become document question-answering.

In Chapter 6, the mode will become tool use.

In Chapter 8, the mode will become workflow automation.

In Chapter 12, these ideas will become a deployed web app.

3.22 Structured Output Habits

Notice that each prompt asks for sections.

For example, /tasks asks for:

Goal:
Tasks:
Risks:
Next Action:

This is not just for readability.

Structured output helps with:

  • User understanding
  • Debugging
  • Evaluation
  • Future automation
  • Consistent formatting

Later, when you evaluate AI outputs, you can check whether required sections are present.

This is a beginner-friendly way to improve reliability.

3.23 Real-World Use Case

A command-line AI assistant can be useful for:

Learning

Ask quick programming questions.

/explain Python decorators

Summarization

Summarize notes or small text snippets.

/summarize [paste text]

Planning

Turn goals into tasks.

/tasks Prepare for a Python interview

Productivity

Get quick explanations without opening a browser.

/ask What is semantic search?

Development

Use it as a base for larger apps.

This project is also useful because it teaches app structure without web deployment complexity.

3.24 Monetization and Portfolio Angle

You can present this project as:

3.25 Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Putting Everything in app.py

If all code lives in app.py, the app becomes hard to test.

Better:

commands.py
prompts.py
assistant.py
llm_client.py

Mistake 2: Mixing Prompt Text with App Loop

Prompt templates should be easy to find and edit.

Store them in prompts.py.

Mistake 3: Calling the API in Every Test

Use a mock client for tests.

Live API calls should be used only for integration testing or final validation.

Mistake 4: No Command Help

Users need to know what commands exist.

Add /help.

Mistake 5: No Exit Command

Always give users a clean way to quit.

Add /exit.

Mistake 6: Unstructured Responses

Vague prompts produce inconsistent output.

Ask for clear sections.

Mistake 7: Ignoring Empty Input

Handle empty input gracefully.

Do not send it to the model.

3.26 Best Practices

Keep app files small and focused.

Use prompt templates.

Use command parsing.

Use structured responses.

Add /help.

Add /exit.

Use a reusable LLM client.

Use a mock client in tests.

Validate missing content before model calls.

Keep API keys in .env.

Document setup steps in README.

3.27 Mini Challenges

Challenge 1: Add a /rewrite Command

Add a command:

/rewrite [text]

It should rewrite text to be clearer and more professional.

Suggested sections:

Improved version:
What changed:

Challenge 2: Add a /quiz Command

Add:

/quiz [topic]

It should generate five beginner-friendly quiz questions.

Challenge 3: Add a /save Feature

Save the last assistant response to:

last_response.md

Challenge 4: Add Conversation History

Store the last three user messages during the current session.

Do not save them permanently yet.

Challenge 5: Add Response Length Options

Support:

/ask short What is RAG?
/ask detailed What is RAG?

Then adjust the prompt based on the chosen style.

Key Takeaways

  • A real AI app needs structure beyond one prompt.
  • Command parsing lets users choose assistant modes.
  • Prompt templates make responses more consistent.
  • Structured outputs are easier to read, test, and improve.
  • A reusable LLM client keeps provider logic separate.
  • Mock clients let you test without live API calls.
  • A command-line interface is a simple way to build useful AI tools.
  • The patterns in this chapter will support RAG, tools, memory, workflows, and deployment later.
